title: Logistic regression: From art to science
contribution: Imposes sparsity, group and selective sparsity, limits on pairwise and global multicollinearity, nonlinear transformations, expert-forced variables, robustness and significance jointly in one MINLO for logistic regression, solves it by outer approximation run as a single branch-and-bound tree through lazy-constraint callbacks with a heuristic first cut, and reports Lasso-level AUC with sparser, less collinear models on synthetic, UCI and TCGA data.
problem_entry: ML+IO+RO: logistic model building is a sequential 'art' (textbooks give no way to weigh competing goals; purposeful selection is laborious and guarantees neither the properties nor the best model); statistics wrote best subset off as intractable after Furnival-Wilson stalled at p = 30; the 450-billion MILO speed-up motivates one joint MINLO whose infeasibility is itself informative (pp. 1-3, 6).
key_idea: Write every desired property as a constraint or objective term on support binaries (cardinality, group equality, z_i + z_j <= 1 for correlated pairs, one transform per variable, forced inclusion, no-good cuts for failed diagnostics, robust loss), loop solve -> validate -> diagnose -> cut, and solve each MINLO by outer approximation with lazy-constraint callbacks and a discrete first-order heuristic as first cut (pp. 2, 4-6, 8-9).
assumptions: Robustified logistic likelihood over a norm ball of data perturbations; big-M with M only required to be large enough; defaults of 5 robustness values, rho = 0.7, condition number 30 and 3 rounds; synthetic x ~ N(0, Sigma) with labels rounded from a noisy logistic score rather than Bernoulli draws; five UCI data sets and TCGA; bootstrap intervals because classical tests do not apply to the robust constrained estimator; post-selection inference admitted as unresolved (pp. 4-7, 11-12, 15).
proof_devices: Theorem 2.1, cited from the group's robust classification paper [6]: robust logistic loss over a norm-ball data-uncertainty set equals a shifted logistic loss with a dual-norm term (p. 4)
maximum-independent-set MIO (6) on the conflict graph of highly correlated pairs gives k_max (p. 5)
no-good cuts sum over S_i of z <= |S_i| - 1 cut a rejected support off the binary hypercube (p. 6)

outer approximation (Duran-Grossmann): MILO reduced master with gradient cuts f(beta) >= f(beta_hat) + grad f(beta_hat)'(beta - beta_hat) alternating with a fixed-support NLO, stopping within epsilon (p. 8)
lazy-constraint callbacks turn the multi-tree outer approximation into a single branch-and-bound tree (p. 9)
first cut at the discrete first-order heuristic solution of [8] (p. 9)
l1 bounding box of radius ||beta0||_1/k around a 180-s solution certifies optimality only within the box when n < p (p. 10)
experiments: NEOS bake-off of six MINLO solvers (default options, 7,200 s cut-off, six synthetic problems up to n = 2000, p = 200): SCIP and Couenne cut off everywhere, none solves Problem 6; tailored method <1-258 s on a different machine (Gurobi 6.0.0, Julia 0.3.3, JuMP 0.7.0); vs Lasso and adaptive Lasso over 10 trials: similar AUC, MINLO at most 7 nonzeros for 5 true (n > p) while Lasso picks 2-4x the true count (n < p), much lower collinearity, weaker true-positive recovery at high noise; TCGA run on 300 Lasso-screened genes (AUC 0.973 vs 0.977); five UCI sets with a 60 s limit per MINLO, MINLO AUC lower on Bank (0.956 vs 0.994), Ozone 8 and Ozone 1; no gaps reported; validation-chosen robustness between 0 and 0.001 in every printed table (pp. 7-16).
positioning: Extends best subset [8] to logistic regression; Sato et al. the only MIO predecessor (piecewise-linear likelihood), so the full MINLO is taken on directly; robustness set apart from distributionally robust logistic regression; outer approximation credited to Duran-Grossmann; repeated 'first' and 'only methodology' priority claims; Lasso as the practitioners' comparator, recast as 'a robust method first and foremost'; purposeful selection named as current practice but never run (pp. 1-4, 7-9, 11, 15-16).
writing: 'From Art to Science' title naming the transplant; abstract stacks properties, the 450-billion figure, a joint MINLO, a suboptimality guarantee and infeasibility as a guarantee; an Aspirations section before the method; a property-to-constraint table; the modeler as 'she'; hedges on timings but optimality wording ('trades these properties off in an optimal way') beside a 60 s limit and no gap columns; the introduction promises more than 30,000 variables while the MINLO ran on 300 screened genes (pp. 1-2, 8, 11-13).
limits_future: Framework, tailored algorithm and evidence; limits: post-selection inference, slow or only local certification for n < p, timings not benchmarks, weaker true-positive recovery under noise, clinically unhelpful TCGA models; future: other robust losses, residual diagnostics, post-selection remedies; no open problem in the conclusion (pp. 6, 8, 10-13, 16).

method_links.note: one joint MINLO replaces purposeful selection's refit loop; discrete first-order heuristic as first cut; solver versions, machine and a 60 s limit stated; out-of-sample duel with Lasso and adaptive Lasso on synthetic data with known truth and on real data. Step 4 slips (Tension T1): no gap or certificate status in any table, and for n < p the certificate is local to an l1 bounding box

belief dated to the 1970s-1980s and conceded as justified then; abstract leads with the figure; the intractability view traced to Furnival-Wilson at p = 30. Step 3 not followed: the 450-billion figure and its 1991-2015 window repeat AoS 2016, and the MILO factor is applied to a MINLO, bridged explicitly by solving through MILO masters

properties written exactly as linear constraints on binaries, but the model leaves the MILO class; off-the-shelf MINLO solvers are measured first, then the algorithm (not the model) is changed so that the MILO solver stays the engine

'the price of interpretability' named for one data set and the correlation cap rerun at one more value (two points, no curve); the robustness knob is chosen by validation AUC and lands between 0 and 0.001, so no price of robustness is shown
the modeler is the owner and purposeful selection her current rule, but the baseline is Lasso and the metric AUC plus sparsity and collinearity

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: post-fit checks (bootstrap significance, condition number above 30) become constraints that cut the offending support off the binary hypercube, then re-solve, up to 3 rounds by default

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: solver bake-off before a tailored algorithm
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: six MINLO solvers run on NEOS with default options and a 7,200 s cut-off on six graded instances; the printed failures motivate the tailored outer-approximation and lazy-callback method

sparsity k and the robustness parameter chosen by AUC on a 25% validation split (selected robustness between 0 and 0.001); the same move in S013 (set, epsilon, alpha by hold-out or CV) and S030 (model and hyperparameters by masked-entry validation)

'From Art to Science' frames regression craft turned into one optimization model; S030 'From Predictive Methods to Missing Data Imputation' and SW5 'From Predictive to Prescriptive Analytics' use the same form

transferable: Encode each modeling desideratum as a linear constraint on support binaries (equal binaries for a group, z_i + z_j <= 1 for a correlated pair, at most one of a variable's transforms, z = 1 for an expert-forced variable) and print a property-to-constraint table (Table 1, pp. 2, 5)
Turn a failed post-fit check (an insignificant coefficient, a condition number above 30) into a no-good cut sum over S of z <= |S| - 1, re-solve, and cap the rounds (p. 6)
Bound the feasible model size first by a maximum-independent-set MIO on the conflict graph of the constraints (p. 5)
Solve a convex MINLO inside a MILO solver: outer-approximation gradient cuts added by lazy-constraint callbacks in one branch-and-bound tree, with the first cut at a heuristic solution (pp. 8-9)
When the lower bound stalls in n < p, restrict to an l1 ball of radius ||beta0||_1/k around a time-limited solution and certify inside it, saying that the certificate is local (p. 10)
Before writing a tailored solver, run the available solvers (NEOS, default options, fixed cut-off) on a graded set of instances and print the failures (Table 2, pp. 7-8)
coauthors: Angela King (Data Scientist, End to End Analytics, at publication)

quotes.text: The belief that MIO approaches to problems in statistics are not practically relevant was formed in the 1970s and 1980s and it was at the time justified.
In fact, what we can be assured of is that the MINLO model trades these properties off in an optimal way given the constraints the modeler specifies.

title: Data-driven robust optimization
contribution: Turns the confidence region of a statistical hypothesis test into a convex uncertainty set whose robust counterpart stays tractable and implies a finite-sample probabilistic guarantee, derives a catalogue of such sets (chi-square, G, Kolmogorov-Smirnov and other goodness-of-fit, forward/backward deviations, marginal order statistics, linear-convex ordering, and bootstrapped versions of Shawe-Taylor-Cristianini and Delage-Ye) with counterparts and separation oracles, optimizes risk allocation across constraints, selects sets by cross-validation, and illustrates them on synthetic portfolio and G/G/1 queueing examples (read as arXiv v2).
problem_entry: RO+CP (AP and SD as testbeds): the uncertainty set decides conservatism and tractability, and existing sets rest on a priori reasoning; with abundant data, keep (P1) tractability and (P2) a probabilistic guarantee for constraints concave in u, but build the set from i.i.d. data so that it is smaller and less conservative (arXiv pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Schema: hypothesis-test confidence region -> convex, positively homogeneous upper bound on the worst-case VaR -> the set with that support function; Theorem 1 shows support function >= VaR is the right condition; pairing a priori assumptions with tests gives each set; an epsilon-independent confidence region gives a simultaneous guarantee that allows optimizing epsilon_j across constraints; set, epsilon and alpha chosen by hold-out or CV (arXiv pp. 4, 10-12, 29-30).
assumptions: f concave in u under a Ben-Tal et al. regularity condition; i.i.d. data; per-set assumptions (finite support; independent components with a known box or bounded support; marginal samples only; joint samples; known R for Delage-Ye); bootstrap thresholds only asymptotically valid; t-test robustness to non-normality; union bounds; CV unproven; both applications synthetic (Natarajan et al. ten-asset model; truncated Pareto/exponential G/G/1 at about 90% utilization) (arXiv pp. 2, 7-8, 12-22, 28-31, 34-36).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: support function >= VaR_epsilon for all v suffices for the guarantee for every f concave in u (strict separating hyperplane) and is necessary for bi-affine f (arXiv pp. 10, 39)
Theorems 2-3: three-line probability chain through the confidence region; an epsilon-independent region gives a simultaneous guarantee that allows optimizing epsilon_j (arXiv pp. 10-12, 39-40)
worst-case CVaR over chi-square and G confidence regions via the Rockafellar-Uryasev CVaR set, Lagrangian duality and a hyperbolic second-order-cone constraint (Theorem 4; arXiv pp. 13, 40-41)
Proposition 1: G and chi-square regions differ by O(n N^-3), by a Taylor expansion of x log x (arXiv pp. 14, 41)

KS worst case by LP duality: the worst-case distribution is the left or right edge of the KS band (Theorem EC.2; arXiv pp. 16, 41-42), combined with the Nemirovski-Shapiro bound (Theorem 5; arXiv p. 16)
forward/backward deviations: three decoupled scalar problems with a closed-form multiplier (Theorem 6; arXiv pp. 19, 43)
order-statistic test for marginal quantiles plus the Embrechts et al. VaR bound with lambda_i = epsilon/d (Theorem 7; arXiv pp. 20-21, 43)
semi-infinite conic duality for the linear-convex-ordering set (Theorem 8; arXiv pp. 22, 44-45)
Delage-Ye region via S-lemma-type duality and Schur complements to an LMI (Theorem 12; arXiv pp. 27, 46-47)
bi-convexity in epsilon by second derivatives (Theorem 13; arXiv pp. 29, 47) and a trust-region LP on shadow prices with kappa = 0.05 (EC.3; arXiv pp. 47-48)
separation oracles in closed form or by line search for cutting-plane use (Remarks 7, 9, 14, 17; arXiv pp. 17, 19, 23, 26)

worst-case Lindley recursion with a closed form by relaxing the integrality of j and KKT conditions for optimized epsilon_j (arXiv p. 34); busy-period truncation with split data, stated as 1 - alpha in the main text but proved as 1 - 2 alpha (EC.5; arXiv pp. 34, 48-50)
experiments: Geometric figures (octagon, independent marginals, four-set comparison) and a threshold table showing bootstrapped thresholds an order of magnitude or more below concentration-inequality ones, which do not apply for N <= 50 or N <= 50,000; portfolio with 10 synthetic assets, N = 500 and 2,000: 5-fold CV picks LCX or CS, confirmed by true 10% worst-case returns (-0.373 and -0.416 vs -1.095 for M), CS best and most stable over 100 repetitions (-0.397 vs CM -0.539), CM calibrated to the same guarantee; G/G/1 median-wait bounds 34.6, 25.8, 14.4 vs a sample Kingman bound of 55.1 at N = 10,000; no solve times, solvers, real data or non-data-driven baseline set reported (arXiv pp. 14, 19-20, 25, 27-36, 48).
positioning: Generalizes Ben-Tal et al.'s phi-divergence sets from uncertain probabilities to general continuous parameters; specialized test uses (Klabjan et al., Goldfarb-Iyengar) said not to generalize; Calafiore-El Ghaoui and Delage-Ye reinterpreted through hypothesis testing and bootstrapped; Campi-Garatti conceded 'more generally applicable' but more conservative for concave f, inapplicable for N < N(epsilon) and dense; Chen-Sim-Sun's deviation set generalized; a priori sets including Bertsimas-Sim called 'theoretically motivated and experimentally validated' (arXiv pp. 1, 3-5, 14-15, 17-18, 23-27).
writing: Abstract: data growth -> schema -> tractable 'both theoretically and practically' -> finite-sample guarantee -> evidence; seven numbered contributions; Table 1 as a one-page map; twenty Remarks carry the computational advice, all proofs in the e-companion; frequent explicit hedges ('Our list is non-exhaustive', 'we cannot prove', no claim that the queueing bounds are the best possible); a one-paragraph conclusion calling the work 'a first step' (arXiv pp. 1, 3-6, 8, 30, 33, 36).
limits_future: Limits: exponential-cone and LMI sets numerically or practically less mature; intersections lose the guarantee and best-objective set choice is biased; hold-out halves the data; the marginal-sample set lacks a simultaneous guarantee; queueing bounds not the best possible; the truncated queueing bound is stated at 1 - alpha in the main text but proved at 1 - 2 alpha. Future: retrofit robust models in information theory, supply chains and revenue management; queueing networks (arXiv pp. 13, 17, 21, 27, 29, 33-34, 50).

method_links.note: sets designed so that the robust counterpart stays in named convex classes (SOC, polyhedral plus one entropy constraint, exponential cone, LMI) with explicit descriptions; the more mature class preferred when sets are close (chi-square over G, CS over the LMI-based DY); duality gives worst-case distributions and the VaR characterization. The stop rule's measured solve time is missing: 'practically' tractable is never timed

confirms SKILL.md's correction that the group set the knob from data: set, epsilon and alpha chosen by hold-out (guarantee kept) or 5-fold CV; but the Bertsimas-Sim budget set is not among the sets and no price curve is printed, only in-sample against true out-of-sample values
sets judged by the decision's performance under the true model, not by their size ('size calculations alone cannot predict performance'), but there is no owner, current rule or real data

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: confidence region -> worst-case VaR bound -> set with that support function; pairing a priori assumptions with tests yields a catalogue of sets with a finite-sample guarantee

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: reinterpret rivals inside your lens, then upgrade them
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Shawe-Taylor-Cristianini and Delage-Ye recast as hypothesis tests, their thresholds replaced by bootstrapped ones that are an order of magnitude smaller, and sets derived for direct comparison

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: retrofit existing robust models with data-driven sets
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: a data-driven set swapped into an existing robust queueing model yields probabilistic waiting-time bounds; suggested for information-theory, supply-chain and revenue-management models
set, epsilon and alpha chosen by hold-out (keeps the guarantee) or 5-fold CV (unproven); shared with S105 and S030

transferable: Calibrate an uncertainty set from data with a guarantee: confidence region of a test -> convex upper bound on the worst-case VaR -> the set with that support function; check the guarantee with the support-function-dominates-VaR condition (arXiv pp. 10, 39)
Replace concentration-inequality thresholds by bootstrapped ones (Algorithm 1) and print a threshold table against N to show the shrinkage (arXiv pp. 8-9, 25)

Allocate risk across m uncertain constraints by optimizing epsilon_j under a simultaneous guarantee, alternating between decisions and epsilon_j with a trust-region LP on shadow prices (kappa = 0.05) so that the objective never increases (arXiv pp. 11-12, 29, 47-48)

Select among candidate sets by evaluating the resulting decisions on a hold-out half, which preserves the guarantee because the halves are independent; fall back to k-fold CV for small N and say that it is unproven (arXiv pp. 29-30)
Calibrate a non-set competitor to the same guarantee before comparing, and audit the cross-validated choice against a known generative model (arXiv p. 31)
Give each set a separation oracle so that the counterpart can run inside a cutting-plane method instead of a heavy conic reformulation (Remarks 7, 9, 17; arXiv pp. 17, 19, 26)
coauthors: Vishal Gupta and Nathan Kallus (Operations Research Center, MIT)

quotes.text: These data have motivated a shift in thinking – away from a priori reasoning and assumptions and towards a new data-centered paradigm.
This experiment highlights the fact that size calculations alone cannot predict performance.

title: From predictive methods to missing data imputation: an optimization approach
contribution: Formulates missing-data imputation as one nonconvex optimization problem over all missing entries with a K-NN, SVM or optimal-tree cost, solves it by alternating block or coordinate descent from incumbent and random warm starts (opt.impute), selects the model by masked-entry validation (opt.cv) and extends it to multiple imputation from mice draws (opt.mi), reporting lower imputation error than five benchmarks on 84 UCI data sets and downstream gains on 10 tasks.
problem_entry: ML+IO+HS: missing data is ubiquitous; joint models break on non-normal or singular data and conditional methods such as pmm have no explicit optimization formulation, unlike other ML areas where optimization drove progress; so pose imputation as minimizing a predictive-model cost with the observed entries fixed (pp. 1-4, 6).
key_idea: One joint problem with three costs (K-NN with binary neighbour assignments, mixed SVM with dummy-coded categorical decisions, optimal-tree leaf co-membership); alternate model fitting and closed-form re-imputation by block or coordinate descent; warm starts from mean, knn, bpca and 5 random draws, keeping the lowest objective; model and hyperparameters selected by hiding a further 10% of entries; multiple imputation from mice-drawn warm starts (pp. 6-20).
assumptions: Continuous columns scaled to unit SD instead of a cost weight; RBF kernels; for continuous variables opt.tree is a single-leaf glmnet regression (no splits), optimal classification trees only for categorical variables; MCAR and NMAR masks imposed on complete data at 10-50%, MAR excluded, validation masks MCAR; 84 UCI data sets (n 23-5,875, p 2-124); MIO certification abandoned as too slow (pp. 6-7, 18, 20-22).
proof_devices: Problem (1): minimize a model-fit cost over imputed values with the observed entries fixed (p. 6)
K-NN cost with binary neighbour assignments, sum_j z_ij = K and z_ii = 0 (eq. 7), and a big-M (k_d) linearization of category mismatch (pp. 9, 11)

alternating minimization: neighbour update by sorting (eq. 8); imputation update by a linear system Q w = R x (block coordinate descent) or closed-form weighted averages over neighbours and reverse neighbours and modes (coordinate descent, eq. 10) (pp. 10-11)
SVM subproblems as dual QPs and per-observation nonlinear integer problems (eqs. 12-14; pp. 13-14)
optimal-tree constraints imported from Bertsimas-Dunn, with leaf means and modes as closed-form updates (eqs. 15-17; pp. 15-17)
termination bound ceil(c0/delta0) from strict descent, no global-optimality guarantee, monotonicity lost with greedy trees (pp. 7, 15)
O(n log n) neighbour assignment as the coordinate-descent bottleneck (p. 31)
experiments: Benchmarks mean, pmm, bpca, knn, iknn; 12 h limit; MAE and RMSE on hidden entries; at 30% MCAR an opt method wins 76.2% of 84 data sets; opt.cv has the lowest geometric-mean MAE (0.100 vs 0.118 at 10%, 0.142 vs 0.172 at 50%; 0.118 vs 0.131 against benchmark.cv at 30%); adjusted Wilcoxon and paired t-tests; downstream (10 tasks, m = 5, 100 repetitions): opt.cv beats benchmark.cv at all levels (+0.0171 accuracy, +0.0237 R2 at 50%), opt.mi beats mice in 8/10; timing (1 thread, 8 GB, 4 h): svm.CD and tree.CD fail on larger sets, knn.CD 1,144-2,582 s at n = 245,057. My checks: the stated 12.1% is about 17% from the printed numbers; opt.mi over opt.cv is 7/10, not 8/10; Table 9's libras rows duplicate the iris rows; missForest not benchmarked (pp. 19-32, 35-36).
positioning: A 19-method taxonomy partly from Liew et al.; mean imputation, joint modelling and pmm criticized; the lineage of optimization-driven ML cited only from the group's own papers (median and sparse regression, optimal trees, robust classification); benchmarks called the most commonly used state of the art; no speed-up figure or intractability belief invoked (pp. 1-5, 18).
writing: Abstract stacks the framework, 'high quality solutions in seconds', 84 data sets and headline numbers (8.3% lower MAE, R2 0.339 vs 0.315, accuracy 86.1% vs 84.4%, 8/10 vs mice); four numbered contributions; the name Optimal Impute for a local method; scaling claims grow from body to discussion (SVM coordinate descent 'in seconds' for 100,000s of points against 'scales relatively poorly' and unfinished runs in Table 9); a From-X-to-Y title (pp. 1, 5, 7, 19, 31-33).
limits_future: Limits: no global optimum; a late rise in MAE suggests overfitting (regularization or early stopping); SVM scaling; multiple imputation slower, pooled and less interpretable; MCAR-only validation masks. Future: other costs (regularizer, L1 or Mahalanobis distances), fast optimal trees, and a global solution of Problem (1), which 'remains an open question' (pp. 7, 22, 31, 33-34).

method_links.note: the warm-start-and-duel half holds: the incumbents' outputs (knn, bpca; mice for multiple imputation) are both warm starts and opponents, with out-of-sample duels on 84 real data sets and adjusted tests, and the baselines get the same CV layer; the exact-solve half is dropped by the stop-rule route (MIO certification too slow, claim narrowed to no global guarantee; Heuristic 3), while the name Optimal Impute keeps the word (Tension T1)
a statistics-owned problem written as an explicit mixed-integer program, but the class serves as a definition, not as a solver target; no MIO solve times reported
imputations judged by the out-of-sample accuracy and R2 of downstream models trained on them, the ML analogue of scoring decisions rather than predictions; no owner or current rule

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: iterative K-NN-style re-imputation rewritten as coordinate descent on an explicit K-NN, SVM or tree cost, which then drives monotone descent, warm-start choice and convergence monitoring; a non-robust analogue of Heuristic 1
model (K-NN, SVM, tree) and hyperparameters (K, C, sigma, cp) chosen by MAE on an extra 10% MCAR mask; also S105 (k and robustness by validation AUC) and S013 (set, epsilon, alpha by hold-out or CV)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: same selection layer for the baselines
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: benchmark.cv picks the best of five benchmarks by the same masked validation before the comparison with opt.cv
imputations scored by the out-of-sample accuracy or R2 of LASSO, SVR, SVM and Optimal Trees trained on the imputed data over 10 tasks and 100 repetitions
'From Predictive Methods to Missing Data Imputation' recasts imputation as prediction-driven optimization; also S105 'From Art to Science' and SW5

transferable: Write a fill-in task as minimization over the missing entries of a model-fit cost with the observed entries fixed; alternate model fitting with closed-form re-imputation and use the objective as the convergence monitor (pp. 6-8)
Create validation data by hiding a further 10% of the observed entries, choose model and hyperparameters by validation MAE, then re-impute under the original pattern (pp. 17, 20)
Give the baselines the same selection layer (benchmark.cv) before comparing composite methods (pp. 17, 20, 24)
Report win counts, geometric means with geometric-SD bands, and multiplicity-adjusted Wilcoxon signed-rank and paired t-tests (Figs. 2-3, Table 5; pp. 24-27)
Score an intermediate product (imputations) by the out-of-sample performance of downstream models across missing levels, for single and multiple imputation (pp. 21-22, 28-30)

Start the local method from each incumbent's output plus random draws and keep the best objective; for multiple imputation, use draws from a probabilistic incumbent (mice) as the m warm starts (pp. 18-19)
coauthors: Colin Pawlowski and Ying Daisy Zhuo (MIT Sloan School of Management and Operations Research Center)

quotes.text: Some conditional specification methods such as pmm are practically reliable, but lack theoretical foundation and have no explicit formulation as an optimization problem.
We ran computational experiments and found that solving such mixed integer problems requires a long time to reach a certifiably optimal solution.
